canberra.title: One dead, two injured after car ‘ploughed’ into group of cyclists in Gungahlin
canberra.snippet: A senior police officer said the scene police were confronted with when they arrived to find a car had crashed into a group of cyclists, ...
canberra.content:
A damaged car was spotted at the scene of the crash on Gungahlin Drive on 27 August 2026. Photo: John Lomnicki.

A senior police officer said the scene police were confronted with when they arrived to find a car had crashed into a group of cyclists, killing one, was “beyond comprehension”.

ACT Policing’s Detective Inspector Mark Steel said a group of five cyclists were riding on Gungahlin Drive, near the intersection with Kosciuszko Avenue, after 6 am on Thursday morning (27 August) when a car “ploughed” into them.

He said members of the public, including two off-duty nurses and an off-duty police member, began performing first aid on the three injured cyclists.

Paramedics arrived but, tragically, a 32-year-old woman died from her injuries at the scene.

Detective Inspector Mark Steel said the woman was originally from Perth in Western Australia. She had moved to Canberra and had friends in the ACT.

“I believe she belonged to a cycle club. They’re a tight-knit bunch and everyone will be hurting at the moment,” he said.

Two male cyclists were taken to hospital, including a 39-year-old who remained in a critical condition on Thursday afternoon. A 34-year-old was treated at the hospital before being released.

The other two cyclists in the group were uninjured.

Detective Inspector Steel said the 40-year-old woman who had been driving the car was not injured and was still assisting police with their inquiries.

“This brings the road toll to 10 for the year now,” he said.

“It’s a tragedy for the families involved. It’s a tragedy for emergency services personnel. It’s a tragedy for the community.”

Police examine the crash scene on Gungahlin Drive on 27 August 2026. Photo: John Lomnicki.

He said both the car and the cyclists had been heading north on Gungahlin Drive at the time of the crash.

“We’re still piecing together how the collision occurred,” he said.

“We believe the cyclists were travelling in the left-hand lane, unimpeded. So, we’re looking at reasons for the collision at the moment.

“At this early time, we’re not looking at speed as a causal factor.”

Detective Inspector Steel thanked the members of the public who stepped in and provided first aid to the cyclists after the crash.

“It’s heartening to know in amongst this tragedy that people stopped to help,” he said.

“We’re praising those members of the public that stopped to render assistance at the scene, because … we could be talking about two fatalities rather than the tragic one at this present time.”

He said cyclists were vulnerable road users and drivers had to look out for them.

“It’s up to us all to look out for each other on the roads,” he said.

Meanwhile, the Canberra Bilbys Triathlon Club posted a statement on social media saying their regular cycling group was involved in the incident on Gungahlin Drive which resulted in the death of one of their members and injuries to others.

“Our club is devastated by these events. Our club is made up of people who love the sport of triathlon, who love getting out there and doing their best, and who support each other through the highs and lows that come with competing in a challenging sport and belonging to a community club,” the statement says.

“Today, and in the coming weeks and months, that support will be more important than ever.

“While some other members of our club were injured and members of the club were present during this incident, we will not be commenting on the circumstances of the accident due to the ongoing police investigation.”

Police are appealing for information or dashcam footage of the cyclists on Gungahlin Drive or of a Hyundai Accent. The Hyundai is light blue in colour with ACT registration YND94Q.

If you can assist police, call Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or visit  Crime Stoppers ACT.

canberra.title: Australians missing in deadly Nepal-Tibet flash floods
canberra.snippet: At least 34 Australians are missing following a deadly flash flood in Nepal and Tibet, which was triggered by a glacial collapse that swe...
canberra.content:
27 August 2026

Start the conversation

The mudslide at the Jilong Port in Tibet. Image: Screenshot.

At least 34 Australians are missing following a deadly flash flood in Nepal and Tibet, which was triggered by a glacial collapse that swept water through the Himalayan border region on Wednesday (26 August).

Anthony Albanese confirmed on Thursday that Australians are missing in the area and that officials from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) are providing consular assistance in Nepal.

“We extend our deepest sympathies to those affected by the significant flooding in Nepal and Tibet, China,” the Prime Minister said.

“Australians in the affected area should follow the advice of local authorities.

“We are aware of a number of Australians in the area and Australian officials are urgently working to confirm their welfare.

“We are liaising with local authorities as well as tour operators. We stand ready to provide consular assistance.”

The Prime Minister later expressed the difficulty in ascertaining information following the tragedy.

“Nepal is a developing country. It doesn’t have the resources that an event like that would have in Australia,” he said.

“So information is difficult. Our thoughts are with all those who will be concerned about their loved ones today.”

At least 165 people have been killed in the floods, which have wiped out entire local villages.

But the area is popular with international tourists, including from Australia, India, the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada.

More than 24 hours after the floods hit, Nepal’s disaster agency reported 823 people remained out of contact, with at least 579 of them being domestic and foreign tourists.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong said the 34 missing Australians were part of separate tour groups and pilgrimages.

She said the Federal Government was urgently trying to determine their situations.

“The government’s priority is to confirm the whereabouts and welfare of these Australians,” Senator Wong said.

“We are currently deploying further DFAT personnel, including crisis response experts to the region to ensure that we do provide the support needed to these posts, particularly our post in Nepal.

“At this stage, access and information are very limited given the scale of the disaster. We will do our best to ascertain whatever information we can.”

The Foreign Minister has spoken to Australia’s ambassador to China and Nepal to convey the government’s support.

Many of those killed and missing were en route to the high-altitude Tibetan pilgrimage site Kailash Mansarovar, which is regarded as holy by Hindus and Buddhists.

Early reports suggested that a 4.4-magnitude earthquake had triggered glacial collapse, but the US Geological Survey subsequently ruled that out.

It said in a statement: “This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake. Additional analysis of nearby seismic stations, long period seismic waves, and satellite imagery led to the determination that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred.”

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor also released a statement on Thursday.

“Our thoughts are with all those affected by the devastating flooding in Nepal and Tibet, including the families who have lost loved ones and those still waiting for news,” he said.

“We are also thinking of the Australians caught up in this disaster and their families here at home.”

Australians in need of emergency consular assistance should contact the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre on 1300 555 135, or +61 2 6261 3305 (if calling from overseas).

canberra.title: Smith not only has some big plans for Bean, he’s calling for a Capital Region Compact
canberra.snippet: As federal elections go, and if they’re on schedule, Australia is approaching the halfway point between the last one and the next. At the...
canberra.content:
Member for Bean, David Smith, would like to see a Capital Region Compact. Photo: Region.

As federal elections go, and if they’re on schedule, Australia is approaching the halfway point between the last one and the next.

At the last one in May 2025, the electorate of Bean in Canberra’s south became the most marginal seat in the country.

It went from a safe Labor seat on a 12.9 per cent margin to one the ruling party barely held onto at 0.3 per cent.

Meet David Smith, the incumbent Labor MP who is determined not to let anything like that happen again.

Before last year’s election, no one outside Bean and few inside knew what Smith looked like.

It seems he was hard-working enough, but he and the Labor Party were hardly working on lifting his profile.

That has all changed since a savvy independent named Jessie Price came within a cat’s whisker of snatching the seat from under Labor’s nose.

Price has already declared that she is running again in the next federal election.

But Smith has embarked on a strategic campaign to raise his profile to let voters in Bean know he can deliver for them.

“It was a really tight race, and I ran into a pretty well organised campaign,” Smith says of the 2025 election result.

“But we didn’t really predict how the Liberal vote was going to collapse in Bean.

“Our primary vote stayed pretty much the same, and everything else around it changed.

“And in the beautiful wonder of preferential voting, it depends on the order in which people were excluded.

“And yes, it is now the most marginal seat in the country.”

Since then, the Member for Bean has been noticeably popping up everywhere.

More community drop-ins; more funding announcements, speeches, op-eds and official openings; more televised questions in Federal Parliament; and even a sit-down interview with Region, which had severely criticised his election performance.

“It was a bit harsh, but hey, that’s politics,” Smith says.

“I think the obvious thing now is our base is still pretty strong, but there are a lot of things to keep delivering right across Bean.

“That means understanding where their needs are at. There’s pressure on the cost of living, and I need to make sure they’re getting their fair share.”

He’s also pushing around a few big ideas for Canberra overall.

Smith has recently touted a review of the Territory’s Self Government Act, and adds that members of the ACT Assembly should have electorate offices closer to their constituents (as in, actually in their electorates – go figure).

The Member for Bean is now going further and proposing a ‘Capital Region Compact’.

In a speech delivered at the ClubsACT Micro-Conference held at the Eastlake Football Club on Thursday 27 August, Smith says Canberra’s uniqueness as the national capital built around the public sector yet also a regional hub for services warrants some special attention.

“The nation asked Canberra to be its capital. The nation should help carry the cost of what that asks of us,” his speech says.

“So today I am proposing the Capital Region Compact. One region. One economy. One future.

“The compact would be an agreement between three governments: the Commonwealth, the ACT and NSW, together with the councils of the region.

“Its engine would be a Capital Region Economic Commission, independently chaired, jointly established, and built on the CRJO’s (Capital Region Joint Organisation) work rather than over it.

“And its destination would be Australia’s first Capital Region Economic Zone.

“Not constitutional change, not amalgamation, not another tier of government, but deliberate integration wherever integration delivers a measurable benefit.”

The ACT and NSW governments have a Memorandum of Understanding for Regional Collaboration, which is renewed every few years as a statement of goodwill.

But Smith urges another approach when it comes up for renewal again.

“We should not sign another memorandum. We should sign the compact,” he says.

“The principle is simple. Where common rules reduce costs without lowering standards, harmonise them.

“Where shared infrastructure unlocks housing and investment, plan it together.

“Where different settings serve a genuine local purpose, keep them. The objective is productivity, not uniformity.”

He says that, in practice, this would mean a qualified tradesperson should not have to prove the same competence twice to work in the same labour market, and a business operating on both sides of the border should provide common information once to a regional concierge.

Priority residential, commercial and industrial projects should be assessed against agreed regional principles and matched with the roads, transport, utilities, schools and health services to support them, “planned as one functional economy rather than through disconnected decisions that push costs and congestion across the border”.

“The region should put one investment proposition to the world, not competing pitches from neighbouring agencies.

“And it means joint strategies for freight, tourism, skills, cyber, defence industries, renewable energy and advanced manufacturing, with responsibility given to whichever institution is best placed to deliver.”

Back to Bean and his chat with Region, Smith says it would be dangerous for him to not take seriously the threat of One Nation.

Pauline Hanson has her eyes on Bean, seeing it as a Labor vulnerability.

That is on top of the renewed vigour the Price campaign will bring to Bean.

“Some of this is about voters who are disaffected and who are feeling a lot of pressure from the current economic environment,” he says.

“But I take them all very seriously … and I have realised there are a number of issues I feel strongly about and it makes sense to get my voice heard on them more often.

“And we definitely need to think about how we fit within our region.”

canberra.title: ‘Girls lose out if St Clare’s goes co-ed’: Why bringing boys to the college is under consideration
canberra.snippet: Catholic education in Canberra is grappling with a question: how to expand co-educational secondary opportunities in the ACT’s sout...
canberra.content:
St Clare’s College has been an all-girls Catholic secondary school since 1965. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Catholic education in Canberra is grappling with a question: how to expand co-educational secondary opportunities in the ACT’s south?

Possible solutions are to expand existing schools, build more or add boys to the all-girls St Clare’s College.

These options were first floated in the recently released Apostolic Action Plan (AAP), which outlined plans to establish a ‘Cathedral Precinct’ and to explore the expansion of co-educational secondary education for families in Canberra’s south.

Then St Clare’s parents and families were sent a letter clarifying that this was on the table.

“Earlier this year parents of children in Kindergarten to Year 5 in Catholic systemic schools in the ACT, Queanbeyan and Yass were surveyed,” St Clare’s principal Dr Ann Cleary wrote.

“The results showed strong demand for more Catholic co-educational secondary options on the south side of Canberra … Land for new non-government schools in the ACT is very limited, so CACGEL [Catholic Archdiocese of Canberra and Goulburn Education Limited] is considering several options to meet this demand.

“The possible future of co-education at St Clare’s College is only one option being considered.”

The other options include expanding or repurposing existing school sites in south-west Canberra or hoping that a land release in NSW will meet the growing demand.

Building new schools doesn’t appear to be an option, with CACGEL arguing the way the ACT releases land to non-government schools is too limited.

St Clare’s College has a community council that represents staff, students and families of its community.

Chair John Norgrove said the majority of feedback received about the proposed options is firmly against a co-ed option.

“Several families have informed me that they would leave St Clare’s if it were to go co-ed,” he said.

“I’m informed that families considering sending their daughters to St Clare’s in 2028 are reconsidering their decision to do so given the current uncertainty, and the co-ed proposal in particular.

“Accepting boys at St Clare’s may increase enrolments, provided the existing families remain at the College and the same number of new girls are enrolled each year, neither of which is guaranteed presently.”

CACGEL is considering piloting the Cathedral Precinct approach by bringing together St Bede’s Primary School, Red Hill; St Benedict’s Primary School, Narrabundah; St Gregory’s Primary School, Queanbeyan; and St Clare’s College, Griffith.

Executive director David de Carvalho wrote the aim was to “further build and refine connections and collaboration between these schools”.

“[This includes] in relation to student transport, specialist teachers, learning support, extension programs and co-curricular activities, with the aspiration of a seamless pathway and recognised community for students from preschool to Year 12,” he wrote.

All of the listed primary schools enrol boys and girls.

The sharing of subject choices, resources and co-curricular activities between St Clare’s and other schools – especially with its neighbour St Edmund’s College – are also discussed in the AAP.

CACGEL does not administer St Edmund’s College and a joint school is not being considered.

Mr de Carvalho said St Clare’s College had a strong reputation for its “warm and welcoming community spirit” and it had the capacity to take on more students.

“Any consideration of change at St Clare’s is not related to any concern about the quality of education, leadership or operations at the school,” he said.

“Rather it is part of a broader system-wide consideration of how CACGEL can best respond to parent choice, changing demographics and the emerging and future needs of families across the Archdiocese.”

He stressed that changes would take place before 2028, and a decision by the board would be communicated in early 2027.

In the meantime, consultation with the community is planned, and a dedicated email address for people to send feedback, questions and concerns has been set up.

Staff are meeting with CACGEL representatives next week, and surveys are expected to be released next month for the St Clare’s College community to fill out.

Dr Norgrove argued that the choice for families to enrol their children in single-sex or co-educational education was an important one, and that bringing boys onto the St Clare’s College campus would be a “significant cultural change”.

“The College promotes female leadership and personal development and provides a place for girls who choose to learn surrounded by other girls,” he said.

“The many benefits of an all-girls College would be removed from the girls and families who have chosen St Clare’s.

“Girls lose out if St Clare’s goes co-ed.”

australia.content:
Week four of the Alan Jones trial zeroed in on a single afternoon 20 years ago, to a luncheon hosted by the veteran broadcaster.

A man referred to in court as Complainant C alleges he was indecently assaulted in the presence of other guests, an allegation Jones denies.

So what have witnesses recalled from that afternoon two decades ago and why has one high profile lunch guest been accused of ‘tailoring’ his evidence?

Nour Haydar speaks to Guardian Australia’s media correspondent, Amanda Meade, to unpack a week of courtroom exchanges, revealing text messages, and an unusual turn by the prosecution.

australia.title: One Nation’s immigration policy is clear as mud – but that ambiguity could be a secret weapon for Pauline Hanson
australia.snippet: The party’s key figures are either unable or unwilling to neatly articulate their migration targets, contradicting one another – and them...
australia.content:
One Nation has experienced a swell in popular support in the past year, and has primarily done so off the back of tough talk on immigration – a policy area almost synonymous with its leader, Pauline Hanson.

But a series of blunders this week show a party unable, or unwilling, to clearly articulate what it would actually do about immigration levels.

Does it want “net zero” immigration, as it boasted for many years? Or does it want a small increase – a net gain of up to 130, 000 people per year – as Barnaby Joyce said emphatically this week?

Let’s step through what key figures have said – and what the party’s policy says.

Officially, the policy listed on the party’s website is a promise to cap visas at 130,000 per year. Whether that would mean a net overseas migration (Nom) target or a permanent visa ceiling is unclear.

Joyce has said this is the party’s Nom cap. On Thursday, Hanson reiterated this.

Nom is the overall gain or loss of population through long-term arrivals and departures. It measures people coming into or leaving the country for a period of at least 12 months over 16 months and thus excludes tourists.

This week David Farley said One Nation’s Nom was 130,000 but that it wouldn’t include an additional 100,000 skilled workers, backpackers and Pacific and Timor-Leste labour through the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (Palm) scheme.

Joyce said that wasn’t right. The former Nationals MP, who defected to One Nation last December, said there were no additional visas hidden from the policy’s headline figure, ruling Farley’s comments out as a rookie mistake.

“When people are new in parliament, they can sometimes get things incorrect,” Joyce said.

The messaging was further muddied after the contribution of the Queensland senator Malcolm Roberts. In a brief interview with the far-right influencer Andre Mamet, known as Ausmaxx, on Tuesday, Roberts appeared to say he supported “net negative migration” – when fewer people enter the country than leave – but he also supported a cap on net migration of 130,000, which implies more people coming than leaving.

“What we’re saying is, every year about 220,000 people leave. I didn’t realise it was so high. And what we’re saying is, we will cap the number of people, net people, [that] come in at 130,000,” Roberts said.

“So if 220,000 people leave … and we allow in 220,000, then that’s – we can’t do that migration. Net migration is complex because it talks about, in 12 months out of only 16 months, the number of people who come in minus the number of people to leave.

“So, if you have 130,000 people coming in, that’s a net migration of minus 90,000. In other words, you lose your population by 90,000. So what we’re saying is the cap on net is 130,000.”

Both Roberts and Hanson have made numerous social media posts supporting “net zero” and net negative migration in the years leading up to 2026.

Hanson confused things further on Thursday when she said the 130,000 figure target was for Nom but didn’t include Pacific labour workers. When asked if that meant there would be more than 130,000 migrants allowed each year under One Nation, she responded: “Correct.”

“Correct, because your Palm workers, rural and regional Australia would die if they didn’t have the workers coming in, and especially the abattoirs and the farmers. So that’s a different program,” she told a News Corp Bush Summit panel.

“These people are given accommodation by the farming sector and the businesses that employ them. So that is not the big impact here. But with immigration, you can’t just tie it to your housing, because infrastructure is another big thing and hospitals and schools and the nursing homes – that has to be all accounted for so it’s just not about houses.”

Hanson added Farley “didn’t understand” and “got confused” when discussing the Palm workers over the weekend.

“As I’ve always said, Palm workers is, the visa-holders that can come into the country. They’re provided accommodation, usually by those on the farms. They’re not taking up the housing. So that’s a totally different matter.”

If the 130,000 figure One Nation commits to is, indeed, a Nom target, it would mean a permanent population increase of 130,000. Each year, about 200,000 people leave the country, including Australians leaving to study and work abroad. Assuming that figure remains consistent, a Nom of 130,000 would mean 330,000 arrive in the country.

However, if One Nation’s policy is a hard cap offering 130,000 visas each year, as the party’s policy says and as Hanson and Roberts argued for less than a year ago, the result would probably lead to negative migration.

The problem with various explanations and interpretations is that it’s impossible for voters to determine which are accurate, and whether others are misleading.

But for a party trying to appeal to its more extreme supporters who argue for hardline policies, it’s a beneficial political tactic, whether intentional or not.

Farley’s comments, which included the suggestion that One Nation’s Nom target was “not too different” from the Albanese government’s, drew a lot of criticism from a number of far-right figures.

Roberts’ interview with Mamet this week could be viewed as an attempt to bring some of them back.

Policy ambiguity has long been Hanson’s secret weapon.

Whether it remains that way under increasing scrutiny of the party, especially under the spotlight of an election campaign, remains to be seen.

  • Sarah Basford Canales is a political reporter for Guardian Australia

australia.title: A new energy scheme gives Australians three hours of free power a day – but there could be an expensive catch
australia.snippet: Solar Sharer program was designed for homes without rooftop solar, but observers say supply and peak use charges are ‘much higher’ Sign u...
australia.content:
A government energy deal that promised three free hours of power to houses without solar panels carries higher charges that make it an expensive option for many households, observers say.

Solar Sharer was switched on in July, with customers in Queensland, New South Wales and South Australia able to opt in to the plan, which includes three free hours of electricity in the middle of day.

Announcing the scheme last year the energy minister, Chris Bowen, said the regulated energy deal would unlock the benefits of cheap and plentiful renewable energy for more households, including those without solar panels or a battery. It was a regulated offer, he said, overseen by the Australian Energy Regulator to “ensure there’s no price gouging going on, it’s in the best interests of the consumers”.

However Gavin Gilchrist, a project manager at Inner West Community Energy, said in his part of Sydney, the supply and peak use charges on Solar Sharer were “much, much higher”, and in some cases nearly double the rate of other market offers.

Gilchrist spent weeks comparing Solar Sharer with multiple energy offers from major retailers – AGL, Energy Australia, Origin and Red Energy – using the government’s Energy Made Easy website, publishing the results in RenewEconomy.

  • Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter

For example, households with one retailer would pay $1.76 in daily supply charges on Solar Sharer on the Ausgrid network, but $0.95 on another plan with the same company. Outside the free power period, the peak rate on Solar Sharer was “almost twice” the rate of the other plan: $0.64 versus $0.33 per kilowatt hour.

Given those rates, he said, most people – especially renters and apartment dwellers, at whom the scheme was aimed – would struggle to get enough value during the free period to come out on top.

“I’m not saying no one can benefit, but you’d have to work very hard to get a benefit from Solar Sharer given the price of electricity outside the three free hours is so much higher, and the daily supply charge is so much higher,” Gilchrist said.

“What was a really good idea to encourage people to use electricity in the middle of the day when we have a glut of electricity on the market, has turned into a fiasco that means virtually no one will benefit.”

Energy Consumers Australia said the design of the scheme forced consumers to make a “complex trade off between free energy in the day and higher prices in all other periods” and some could be worse off if they switch.

Solar Sharer is a regulated plan with parameters set by the Australian Energy Regulator, but a spokesperson for Bowen said it was “up to retailers to explain why they don’t want to pass on the benefits of free electricity to the consumers who can take it up”.

“The government and energy regulator continues to encourage households to check if they’re on the best energy offer, and see if solar sharer is right for them,” the spokesperson said.

Tristan Edis, a director with the consultancy Green Energy Markets, said default or regulated offers like Solar Sharer were “bad offers, almost always”.

People interested in an energy plan with a free power period, and with the capacity to shift their electricity use, should consider competitive retail market offers, he said, adding that the government could help people weigh up those options by updating Energy Made Easy to help people to find and compare “zero-cost, middle-of-the-day offers”.

Heidi Lee Douglas, the chief executive of Solar Citizens, said Solar Sharer was meant to be about sharing the benefits of abundant solar power more broadly.

“So many people we thought would benefit from the Solar Sharer offer are not,” she said. “We’re calling on the regulator to investigate whether the policy is actually delivering what Australians were promised.”

australia.title: ‘Lots of my friends are missing’: fears and prayers as Australia’s Nepali diaspora desperately seek answers after flood
australia.snippet: As the community scrambles to check on loved ones, some hear from family members who fled to safety, while others pray for good news Get ...
australia.content:
When Suman Shrestha opened his phone at work and saw vision of a thick, muddy wall of flood water smashing into towns in his country of birth, he almost did not believe what he was seeing.

“It was awful – I called my family to see if this was really happening and to see if the news reports were right,” says Shrestha, who moved to Australia from Kathmandu in 2017.

It wasn’t long until the truth hit home. Like many of the 210,000 people who were born in Nepal but now call Australia home, Shrestha has spent the last 24 hours scrambling to find out if his loved ones are safe.

“I can see that lots of my friends are missing,” says Shrestha, who now lives in Gosford. “We can’t get in contact with them because the communications have been cut off in that area.”

Nearly 1,500 people are missing and at least 165 have been killed in Nepal and Tibet by the flood, which was caused by an avalanche of ice and rock on Wednesday. At least 34 Australians have been reported missing in the area, including a child as young as 11.

Shrestha fears two friends who he grew up with in Nepal may now be dead. They were working as tour guides and were leading a group of tourists on a trek in the area devastated by the flood water.

“It’s hard,” Shrestha says. “One of them is my close friend’s brother. The other lived near my home in Nepal … I know them well.

“Their families know that they have been trekking in this area and now they cannot contact them,” he says. “They were in contact until 9am on Wednesday, Nepal time, now they can’t reach them.”

Shrestha says their families in Nepal are constantly trying to contact the government for help, but there is little they can do.

“It’s hard for the government, as there is no proper way to reach them and no proper search can be done at the moment,” Shrestha says.

In Sydney, Sujan Tamang is growing increasingly worried about his uncle and aunt. He has not spoken to them since Wednesday. His sister, who works at a hydropower plant in Nepal, had to run from the flood water to safety. He says some of her colleagues are now dead.

When he first watched the footage from Nepal, Tamang could identify the buildings being swept away as if made of straw.

“When I saw that video, it was a very bad feeling,” said Tamang. “That house, that place, I know every place and I know every person. I have entered their houses, we have eaten together, slept together, we were like family.”

Vasan Srinivasan is also scrambling for answers.

The chief executive of the Mental Health Foundation Australia is searching for 15 Australians who travelled to Nepal on a pilgrimage organised by the Himalayan Glacier tour group. All but one are Sydney-based members of his religious group, Australia Bharatha Brahmin Samaj.

“I’ve been very busy using all my contacts, including Nepali community leaders here in Australia,” says Srinivasan, who has also called on Australian ministers for help.

“I am concerned about their wellbeing … Hopefully, God can give me the privilege to get them back to Sydney.”

Chiran Tiwari, the president of the Nepalese Australian Welfare Society, says it has been a chaotic and stressful time for members.

“They are trying to call whoever is in the nearest area that they are able to contact,” Tiwari says. “It is a very big disaster.”

As the Nepali community waits for the full scale of the disaster to become clear, more than 100 people gathered for a special prayer service at a Buddhist temple in Melbourne’s north-western suburbs.

The service’s host, the Australian Nepalese Multicultural Centre, said the community gathered “in prayer for those who have lost their lives, those who remain missing, the injured and all families affected by this disaster”.

Others who feel helpless have turned their attention to fundraising, including for the Nepali government’s disaster relief fund.

“At the moment, we are in the initial phase of our community campaign here in Victoria, trying to raise awareness and mobilise support for those affected by the disaster in Nepal,” said Prem Raj Upreti, the president of the Nepalese Association of Victoria.

On Thursday afternoon, Nepal’s T20 cricket team paused for a moment of silence before playing at Darwin’s Gardens Oval.

In a statement, the Northern Territory’s minister for multicultural affairs, Jinson Charls, said it was providing support to the players and team officials.

“We stand shoulder to shoulder with our local Nepalese and Tibetan communities and will provide all support as necessary,” Charls said.

world.title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’
world.snippet: Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regime The UK Foreign Offic...
world.content:
The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism.

Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel.

Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”.

The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid.

The government of President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi has faced allegations that it frequently arrests relatives of political critics to put indirect pressure on the dissidents to end their overseas criticism of his rule or of state corruption. Much of Mona’s activism focuses on alleged cases of corruption inside the security services or public utilities, a highly sensitive subject in Egypt.

Arfan Rashid, the lawyer acting for Eman’s husband with whom she has four children, says that unlike Mona his wife has never been involved in politics, and had gone to Cairo two months ago to look after her ill mother after the arrest of her two brothers.

“There is ample evidence that Eman has been arrested to silence Mona,” Rashid said. He added that Eman had told the security officials she was no longer in contact with her sister, and that many family members had repeatedly asked her to stop her political activism in the UK, but to no effect.

Mona confirmed to the Guardian that she had been asked to halt her activism by other family members, including to take down her YouTube videos.

But she added: “I have done nothing wrong nor broken any law … I am a very strong woman, but it is very traumatic for me since 11 or 12 children are without their parents. It is a horrible situation, but the Egyptian government will not stop if I appear weak. The government is close to collapsing.”

Rashid said the UK government had recognised the practice of “punishment by proxy” in Egypt in its country profile policy and information note published in March 2026. Human Rights Watch and the House of Commons library warned in 2021 of an escalating pattern in which Egyptian family members of critics living abroad were being targeted.

Mona runs a YouTube channel in the UK that has 130,000 subscribers. She is also active on X, making specific and controversial claims about government officials.

The UK’s Foreign Office representation in Cairo has asked for access to see Eman but has not yet received a positive reply.

Eman’s husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, has said Egyptian police and security officers attended the family home where she was staying a few days before the arrest, and demanded that Eman tell Mona to stop publishing material against the Egyptian government.

On X, Mona has claimed as many as five members of her family have been detained or harassed by the Egyptian authorities. She wrote: “Kinship is something beyond my family’s will, and I invite them to disown me to save themselves from this despicable, illegitimate dictator. I am the one opposing Sisi, not five individuals from my family. This is a crime against humanity that does not lapse with time.” She has lived in the UK for 18 years.

Eman became a British citizen through marriage. Her lawyer has asked whether Alistair Burt, the UK’s new envoy on complex consular cases, should be asked to intervene by the Foreign Office. Burt was appointed a month ago and has been tasked with working to secure the release of British citizens held abroad.

Burt has already met Gurpreet Singh Johal, the brother of Jagtar Singh Johal, who has been detained by the Indian authorities for nearly nine years without a conviction.

The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.

world.title: South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs
world.snippet: Bird eggs intercepted in homemade incubators at Johannesburg airport as officials try to halt wildlife trafficking South African police h...
world.content:
South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking.

A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement.

The ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species.

Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

South Africa is battling wildlife smuggling on several fronts, from poached rhino horns and the bones of illegally farmed tigers to abalone shellfish and succulent plants.

The environment ministry said: “The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs pose a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare. Eggs are often concealed in improvised incubation devices and transported under conditions that significantly compromise their viability and endanger the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings.”

Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria are incubating the seized eggs, the ministry said. “Several of the rescued eggs have successfully hatched and the chicks are receiving intensive veterinary and husbandry care to maximise their chances of survival,” the statement added.

The ministry said the arrests were carried out after a “joint intelligence-driven operation” led by its Environmental Management Inspectorate, known as the “Green Scorpions”, and police intelligence, border and endangered species units.

South Africa punishes the illegal export of Cites-listed species with a fine of 10m rand (£460,000), up to 10 years in prison or both.

world.title: Mpox is back – and in new countries. How can this outbreak be contained?
world.snippet: The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly...
world.content:
A fresh outbreak of mpox in Guinea Bissau – the country’s first – means the virus formerly known as monkey pox is back in the headlines. So what has changed?

Since 2022, there have been almost 190,000 lab-confirmed cases of mpox reported worldwide in 145 countries. Before then, outbreaks of mpox tended to be relatively small and in a handful of African countries, where the viral infection was known to be endemic.

What is mpox?

Mpox is an infectious disease that typically starts with flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills and aching muscles. These are followed by a distinctive rash, beginning as raised spots that turn into blisters filled with fluid before forming scabs.

It used to be called monkeypox, because the virus was first discovered in captive monkeys in 1958. But during an international outbreak in 2022, there were concerns that the name was fuelling racist and stigmatising language on and offline, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to recommend changing it to mpox.

It is endemic to many parts of Africa, with outbreaks historically starting when people ate meat from infected wild animals. But in recent years it has spread beyond the usual areas, with sustained chains of human-to-human transmission. The Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said this month that mpox was on course to become endemic in the US.

Why is it spreading to new countries?

There are, broadly, two types of mpox, known as “clades”. Clade I was once called the “Congo Basin clade” and clade II the “West African clade”.

The latter sparked a major global outbreak in 2022 when it appeared to undergo some changes that allowed it to spread more efficiently from person to person. It is passed on via close contact – in that outbreak, mostly by sexual contact, with men who have sex with men at the highest risk.

In June 2024, researchers raised the alarm about a new variant of clade I in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which also appeared to be spreading more easily between people. That grew into another major international outbreak, which was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO on 14 August 2024.

“Emergence of mpox in more countries in west Africa is to be expected,” said Prof Michael Marks, of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and University College London hospital. “Mpox outbreaks have now been declared in a number of countries in the region, including Guinea and Sierra Leone within the last 12 months.

“Mpox spreads by close physical contact. This makes it suitable to spread in a variety of different contexts, such as in close sexual networks, as was seen during the 2022 global pandemic, or areas where many people are living closely together such as settings with refugees and internally displaced people, as was seen in the DRC outbreak over the last few years,” Marks said.

What happened to those two big outbreaks?

The 2022 outbreak was declared a public health emergency in July that year. After contact-tracing and mass vaccination programmes, the status was lifted in May 2023. There had been about 90,000 infections.

The 2024 outbreak had its international public health emergency status lifted in September 2025, not because the disease had disappeared but because numbers of cases and deaths were declining and officials felt the situation had become better controlled.

If genetic testing reveales a new variant, or surveillance suggested an outbreak was spreading particularly fast, making people particularly sick or proving more deadly, global health authorities would be likely to step in again.

How worrying is the new outbreak?

Cases had not been reported in Guinea Bissau before this outbreak. Unicef said it was concerned that of 46 suspected cases, 23 were children aged under 15 and most of those were aged under four.

“The concern about children is that they are at the highest risk of severe disease and death from mpox,” said Dr Aula Abbara, a senior lecturer at Imperial College London and adviser to Médecins Sans Frontières UK. “Young children can become much sicker than healthy adults.” 

However, she cautioned that the apparent over-representation of children in the outbreak data should be interpreted carefully. She said: “There may also be some bias in the data. Families are often more likely to seek healthcare for a sick child than for an adult, particularly in a resource-constrained setting with a fragile health system, such as Guinea-Bissau.”  

Marks added: “Children have close physical contact with their parents and with each other, and in settings such as Guinea-Bissau are often living in cramped conditions, which make close physical contact and transmission more likely.”

Confirmed cases do not appear linked to each other, which suggests the virus is circulating more widely in the community and there are unidentified cases.

Are there vaccines and treatments?

The WHO recommends two vaccines, which can be given to people at high risk or offered to people who have been in contact with a known case to prevent further spread. The question is where they are available.

Marks said: “The major challenge remains that supplies of vaccines are best in high-income countries but worst in low-income settings, where the need and conditions for mpox transmission are highest.”

A new global stockpile is due to be launched within weeks, which should mean vaccines can be deployed more rapidly to quell outbreaks. Officials also hope it will allow manufacturers to plan ahead and produce more of the jabs by providing a clear, concrete demand.

An antiviral called tecovirimat did not appear any better than a placebo when tested on patients with mpox clade I in the DRC, although the question of whether it might help some immunocompromised patients – such as those living with HIV – remains open. That trial did show, however, that giving patients good, supportive care dramatically improved their chances of survival.

While vaccines remained an important tool for outbreak control, basic supportive care could be lifesaving, Abbara said. She added that strengthening surveillance, testing, contact tracing and broader public health measures would be critical to understanding and containing the outbreak.

“Vaccines are important, but outbreaks are not controlled by vaccines alone,” she said. “Early detection, contact tracing, supportive care and strong public health surveillance remain absolutely essential.”

world.title: Moringa lattes and tigernut kebabs: the Ghanaians ‘taking back the power’ of their food
world.snippet: In Ghana, a grassroots movement is championing nutritious, homegrown, climate-resilient produce, rather than western imports After three ...
world.content:
After three years at catering school in Accra, Abiro Wisdom was certain of one thing – he did not want to go into catering. At least not the route that he might be expected to take. His course had prepared students for working in international hotels, focusing on French, Italian and Mexican cuisine. The nutritious, homegrown food that Wisdom had eaten while growing up in Bolgatanga, northern Ghana, did not feature at all.

“I didn’t see myself there,” he says of the big chain hotels. “I felt I wouldn’t be myself working there – I wouldn’t be able to talk about the food from where I come from.”

Wisdom instead joined the Ghana Food Movement (GFM), which was founded in 2019 – the year he graduated – and quickly became a champion for Indigenous foods. He says: “We’re a community of food lovers, of believers in the potential of Ghanaian food.”

Ghana imports at least half of its food and is heavily influenced by foreign cuisine and ingredients, but Wisdom believes northern Ghana, the country’s agricultural heartland with its huge variety of nutritious and climate-resilient crops and vegetables, could be the secret to the country’s broken food system.

The GFM was initially a network of volunteers interested in food systems – chefs, farmers, entrepreneurs and experts in food security. In the early days they met in cafes and set up events in whatever space they could find to deliver three-course meals highlighting a single crop and the diverse ways it can be used.

“[Traditionally] we make tigernut milk, but you can make so many different things, for example tigernut burgers and tigernut kebabs,” says Aimee Wallin, the group’s Malian-Swedish co-managing director. “We want people to taste what we are about, not just talk about what we are about.”

The group has been registered as a non-profit organisation for the past five years and now has its own kitchen where it brainstorms new recipes, many of them thought up by Wisdom. It runs monthly pop-ups and dine-and-dance nights, as well as panel discussions and recipe testing events for chefs and local businesses. Wisdom says: “We might brainstorm ideas around a single food, such as moringa leaves, to show how it’s possible to sell – and make a profit from – dishes and drinks using Indigenous ingredients.”

The GFM has started working with schools, helping children appreciate local ingredients.

Wisdom hopes this multi-pronged approach will help instil more national pride in Ghanaian food. “My goal is that we have a generation of chefs who believe in Ghanaian food and its own identity,” he says.

“I’ve come to understand how food contributes to politics, to the economy, how it contributes to self-identity. [Now I can] trace the impact of food on our society, on our land, to the sea, to the farmer, down to how the food gets to the market, then to our plates. As chefs, we have to be able to tell the story of the food.”

This month the group won a Champions of Change title in the 50 Best Restaurants Awards in recognition of the transformational work it is doing.

Foreign, colonial influence has played a heavy role on African food systems, when ruling powers dictated land should be used for cash crops for export, such as cocoa or peanuts, at the expense of food for local consumption.

At the same time, they put more value on imported ingredients such as rice, disrupting the sustainability of countries’ food systems. The impact has continued to modern times, making African countries heavily reliant on imports and vulnerable to price shocks when wars or other crises disrupt shipping.

But, as Wisdom discovered at university, there is also a lingering cultural influence, with western food still taught in culinary institutes and sought after in restaurants.

“The narrative has always been that our practices are wrong and the west’s practices are right. It’s just super-stupid. Why would you do that when you can just grow your own food?” says Wallin.

“Part of the postcolonial agenda is for us to still have to depend on other countries. If it’s not to buy their products, to buy their vegetables, then at least we need to buy their seeds and their pesticides and their fertilisers,” says Wallin, who points out that many of the local ingredients they champion do not need extra agricultural inputs because they are adapted to the local environment.

“The one who feeds us will control us and that’s how it is today. So, if we want to control ourselves, we also need to feed ourselves. It’s power. Taking back the power of our foods and using it to our advantage.”

For younger Ghanaians there is a new international pull towards heavily advertised trends and social media fads such as matcha lattes, bubble tea and smash burgers.

Wallin says that also offers a culinary opportunity – to earn the interest of young people, by offering alternatives, replacing matcha with moringa lattes or making shawarma out of tigernut instead of meat.

Both Wallin and Wisdom believe that their movement has the urgent task of saving Ghana’s food heritage before knowledge is lost.

“If we want to talk about what our future food system should look like,” says Wallin, “we need to talk to our grandmas, to our grandpas, to the farmers out in the communities because they sit on that knowledge. If we don’t talk to them now, it’s going to be too late. So it’s really now or never.”

world.title: Prince Harry quits board of wildlife charity after rangers’ human rights abuses
world.snippet: Spokesperson for Duke of Sussex says he remains an ‘active and avid supporter’ of African Parks’ mission The Duke of Sussex has stepped d...
world.content:
The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of a major African wildlife charity that had been at the centre of a human rights controversy.

Prince Harry’s spokesperson confirmed he was no longer a trustee of African Parks, which admitted last year that human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in the Republic of the Congo.

The charity’s admission followed an independent review into allegations made by members of the Baka community.

In a 2024 report published by the Mail on Sunday newspaper, community members accused African Parks rangers of beating, waterboarding and raping locals to stop them from accessing their ancestral forests, which are now in a conservation area.

After the review, African Parks published a statement acknowledging that human rights abuses occurred in the Odzala-Kokoua national park, which it manages. It said that it had improved its safeguarding processes both at the park and institutionally.

A spokesperson for Harry said the duke, who was president of the charity for six years before he became a member of its board of directors in 2023, remained an active and avid supporter of African Parks.

“The duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board,” the spokesperson said.

“His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks’ mission.”

Survival International, a global human rights charity that campaigns for the rights of Indigenous people, had called on Harry to step down as a member of the board.

Caroline Pearce, the executive director of Survival International, said it was “outrageous that for 10 years Prince Harry has served African Parks” while people working for it had “been responsible for abuse and violence against Indigenous people. His departure doesn’t undo that record — African Parks itself must now be held accountable, and must abandon this model of fortress conservation for good.”

Founded 26 years ago, African Parks manages more than 20m hectares (50m acres) in partnership with 13 African governments and hundreds of local communities.

African Parks expressed “deep gratitude” to the duke on concluding his tenure after his 10-year commitment to the organisation.

“His relationship with the organisation dates back to Malawi in July 2016, when he supported one of the largest elephant translocations in history. He served as president for six years before being appointed a member of the board of directors,” it said.

“Over the years, the duke has brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa. The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks’ work.”

The announcement comes as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are due to relocate to the UK from California with their children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.

Former Suits star Meghan is said to be pursuing an acting role, with reports she has been in talks about a role in the third series of Guy Ritchie’s Netflix hit The Gentlemen, swiftly followed by other reports that the deal was off.

The couple are understood to be planning an “extended stay” in the UK, and their children are already enrolled in school, but it has not been confirmed for how long.
